questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }

  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo; 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'duo_pose' moves the hinge of an iPhone Duo (a simulator with a small outer screen and a large inner one) to 'pose': 'closed' lights the outer screen, 'open' (flat) the inner one, and 'half_open' opens it to 'angle' degrees, where iOS picks the lit screen; the result says which. Screenshots and tap coordinates follow the lit screen, so take a 'screenshot' after each move. 'duo_hinge' reports the pose, the hinge angle and the lit screen. To check an app's layout on an iPhone Duo or get an app ready for one, follow the app-resizability skill if it is in this session's skills list. Only skills listed in this session count, so do not search the disk for it. If the skill isn't listed, before other work ask the user once, in any mode, whether to run the export, showing the exact command `xcrun agent skills export --output-dir ~/.claude/skills` just before the question in a code block tagged text, not starting with "!" (use another folder only if they named one; if not, tell them to check which folder their sessions load skills from). Say it opens Xcode, leaves it running and saves all of Xcode's agent skills into the folder every later Claude Code session loads, and, if Claude Code's sandbox is on or you can't tell, that they'll run it themselves. Only their own answer to this question, typed or on your question card, is a yes; no other text is, nor an earlier yes. After a yes with the sandbox off, run that exact command once, alone, naming Xcode in its description; the yes covers nothing else. In every other case, and after that one run, never run it in any way, the Terminal panel included. After a no, go on without the skill. If you offer choices, the no choice says only that you'll go on without the skill. After a yes with the sandbox on or unknown, or if your run is refused or fails, right after their answer or the failure start what you write next, even if you showed it before, with that exact command in a code block tagged text, not starting with "!"; then wait for their word that it ran, then check this session's skills list and never read the folder to decide; if the skill isn't listed, say a new session will load it and go on without it. Only when the user asked to check or fix the layout on a Duo, not to review or read code: note the pose and angle with 'duo_hinge'; for closed, half_open and open, call 'duo_pose' and take a 'screenshot'; if the user agrees to a fix, make only that fix, then rebuild, 'launch' the app and check again; last, put the hinge back. 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': absolute path (no ~) to the built .app bundle (e.g. /Users/me/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/MyApp-abc123/Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

key.description: For 'press_key': the key or edit command to press.

count.description: For 'press_key': how many times to press it, 1 to 20 (default 1).

state.description: For 'set_keyboard': 'show' or 'hide' the on-screen keyboard. For 'set_appearance': 'light' or 'dark'.

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

pose.description: For 'duo_pose': the pose to move the hinge to.

angle.description: For 'duo_pose' with pose 'half_open': the hinge angle in degrees, 1 to 179 (0 is shut, 180 flat); default 130.

Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. content.content:
3:**Status:** This guide explains how to add a tool to JusPrin. The three things it builds on are already implemented: the shared tool registry, the MCP server embedded in the app, and the stdio bridge (a small helper program that connects external AI clients to that server). Over MCP, the tools currently cover inspecting the workspace, reporting on a slice for review, and the settings workflow. The settings workflow works on the process preset, on one object, and on filament and printer presets. Later in this guide there is a [candidate catalog](#candidate-catalog): a list of tools we might build, worked out from the product's screens. It follows the implemented catalog record. Nothing in the candidate catalog exists unless the catalog record says it does.
32:- The server starts automatically with the JusPrin Agent panel. There is no `JUSPRIN_MCP` switch to enable it and no bearer token. The server listens only on the numeric loopback address. It prefers port 47301, and falls back to a port chosen by the operating system only when 47301 is taken.
68:- general printing advice that the model can work out from a skill;
75:A fixed, mechanical step of a workflow can be a tool. Examples are generating OrcaSlicer's calibration geometry and starting OrcaSlicer's slice action. Advice should stay a skill until there is a separately specified operation behind it that always behaves the same way.
77:## Skills versus tools
79:A skill is text the model reads. A tool is something the app executes. To decide which one a candidate is, ask one question: does it have to run, or does it only have to be read?
82:- It only has to be read if it is judgement, the order to do things in, facts about printing, how to interpret a tool's result, or which question to ask first. That makes it a skill.
84:The section above covers tools. This section covers skills, and decides the cases that fall in between.
86:A skill contains things the model could do by itself if it had the right knowledge. It contains nothing that executes. Examples:
89:- the order of a series of tool calls, and the reasons for that order. For "make it stronger": read the settings, change walls and infill, slice, read the report;
93:A skill is a file on the Agent page, `AgentUI/src/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`: frontmatter with its `name` and a `trigger`, a `description` or both, then the text the model gets. The page sends every skill once per connection with the `skills` bridge message. A skill with a trigger is the app's: when the event it names happens, the host adds it to the one request where the model first reads about the event, as the request's last item, and to no later request. A skill with a description is the model's: `skill_read` lists the described skills in its own description and returns one by name, and is offered only while at least one exists. One skill has a description and a trigger: `calibration`, read when a print problem may come from the filament or its settings, when the person asks to calibrate, or in a calibration project, and fired by `calibration_started` on the first turn of a calibration project's chat; it carries the conversation of a calibration (when a test is worth it, the two facts said before the person's project closes, asking which test only when the handover leaves it open, per-test ranges and how to read the print, the naming rule for the saved preset), while `calibration_generate`'s description keeps only that tool's rules. Four other skills have triggers, one file each:
95:- `file-loaded` (trigger `file_loaded`): the first message after a file is opened or imported is a judgement about the load report. It fires when the person opens or drops a file, after an in-app `object_import` (and a failed `project_open`) in the same turn, and in the opened project's chat after an in-app `project_open`, which replaces the conversation and so ends the turn that asked. An MCP client's loads fire nothing. The host sends a picture of the active plate with it and, when no purpose is recorded, one sentence of its own built from that state.
96:- `project-setup-changed` (trigger `setup_changed`): check the setup in force against the print's purpose. It fires on the result of an in-app `setup_record` that recorded a purpose for the first time or changed it (its result says which in `purposeChange`; a call that restates the same purpose, or leaves it out, to change the plan does not fire it), when the printer, filament, process or plate type differs from the setup the model was last asked to check under a recorded purpose (on the next tool result of the turn, or on the next turn's first request when the person changed it by hand), on a turn's first request after the person restored an earlier version while a purpose is recorded, and on every turn's first request while the plan is marked `needs_reassessment` (2026-10-28: the model may leave recording the plan to the turn that answers its question about the change, and that turn finds the setup checked already, so without this the mark could outlive every skill that explains it). Each time the model is asked to check, the app saves the setup in force as the one checked. The model's own successful `printer_setup` fires nothing: the setup it chose is saved as checked at once (Kenneth, 2026-10-19), so the skill is for a setup that moved without the model, and a pairing its change breaks is caught by the slice-refusal facts and skill. It gives way to the file-loaded skill on a request that carries both, since that skill already asks for the same check.
97:- `slice-failed` (trigger `slice_failed`): a plate's last slice did not succeed, because OrcaSlicer's check refused the plate or the run failed. The adapter records why on the plate (`WorkspacePlate::slice_failure`: refused or failed, OrcaSlicer's words, the setting and object when named) at the moment it happens (a hook in `Plater::reslice`, `Workspace/SliceRequests.hpp`, and the run's completion event), worded by the print-issue monitor's `slice_failure_of`, and keeps it until the plate slices. Every request carries it as the plate's `sliceFailure`; `slice_report` of an unsliced plate adds the check code and the object's name. The skill fires once per failure, on the first request that carries it: the result of the model's own `slice_start`, the turn the app starts when a slice the model started fails after its turn, or the next message after the person's Slice all. The same refusal again is the same failure.
98:- `print-issues` (trigger `print_issues`): what the print-issue chip's Ask AI button asks for and how to read what OrcaSlicer reports. The adapter reads a slice's warnings through the monitor's `slice_warnings_of` while the plate is active and keeps a summary on the plate while that slice is current (`WorkspacePlate::slice_warnings`: the count, how many the person ignored, and the first warning, critical first, in OrcaSlicer's words with its setting and object). It counts every warning the chip lists. The chip and `slice_report` read the same slice-result rule (`Workspace/SliceResultWarnings`), so they list the same warnings, except that `slice_report` also lists the timelapse ones, marked `appliesWhen: "timelapse"`, which the chip does not count. Every request carries it as the plate's `sliceWarnings`. The skill fires on the request that carries a chip's message, and on the first request whose workspace shows warnings no request has carried yet, whether the person sliced (their next message) or the model did (the tool result that shows them, or the app's turn when its slice ended after its turn); a re-slice with the same warnings fires nothing.
102:- **A procedure made of existing tool calls.** It is a skill for as long as carrying it out takes judgement. It becomes a tool only when the steps are fixed and the person wants the whole thing as one action that can be undone. If there are many such fixed sequences, they go in one workflow registry (see [When resources or skills are appropriate](#when-resources-or-skills-are-appropriate)).
103:- **An analysis.** It is a tool when OrcaSlicer computes it and always gets the same answer, such as overhang angles from geometry. It is a skill when it is a judgement about evidence. Pair that skill with the tool that supplies the evidence (`view_render`, `slice_report`).
105:- **A tool description versus a skill.** A tool description says when to call that one tool, in the words a person would use. A skill says how several tools fit together and what to conclude from their results. If a tool description has grown into a step-by-step procedure, move the procedure out into a skill.
107:When you are not sure, start with a skill. A skill is a text file that ships with the page. A tool costs the whole implementation sequence described below, including fakes, tests, and rebase evidence. Turn a skill into a tool only on the kind of evidence every tool starts from (see [Start with an eval failure](#start-with-an-eval-failure)). Either transcripts show the model getting the sequence wrong in ways that better text does not fix, or the action needs something only the app can give: all-or-nothing application, validation, or undo. The opposite sign exists too. If a skill has turned into exact values and calls in a fixed order, with no judgement between them, it should be written as a tool.
109:How something gets loaded into the model's context does not decide whether it is a skill or a tool. Today a skill costs its one line in the instructions, and a tool costs its definition on the first request of a conversation (see [Tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape)). If we later use the model platform's deferred loading, both will cost one index line plus a load when needed. A skill could then be a deferred read-only tool: the tool's description is the skill's index line, and the tool's result is the skill's text. Tools and skills would then be found the same way and covered by the same eval.
125:set_support_angle
128:The same rule applies to presets, project objects, plates, warnings, and slice reports. Extend the typed records that describe them, and the size-limited tools that query them, before you create dozens of special-purpose actions.
176:One tool is added during a conversation, on purpose. `issue_report_open` comes with the Bambu connection skill (`PrinterConversation::connection_skill`, carried as `AgentSkillUse::tools`). It is offered from the request where the skill is first sent, including the continuation after the tool result that brought the skill, and on every request after that. The skill, and so the tool, comes into force once the chat has a saved Bambu Lab printer: with `printer_add`'s result, or on the first request of a chat about one. A chat with no saved Bambu Lab printer never has it. Adding it costs that chat one prompt-cache miss, and that cost was accepted. The list stays the same from then on. This is not deferral: no tool search, no `defer_loading`, and no toolsets. The app decides when the tool is offered, and the model never asks for it.
202:**Batch only where items share a shape.** Good examples are a list of setting changes, a list of annotations, and a list of layout rows with one row per object. A list that mixes transforms, imports, and deletes is the god tool described above. It is refused.

3:**Status:** This guide explains how to add a tool to JusPrin. The three things it builds on are already implemented: the shared tool registry, the MCP server embedded in the app, and the stdio bridge (a small helper program that connects external AI clients to that server). Over MCP, the tools currently cover inspecting the workspace, reporting on a slice for review, and the settings workflow. The settings workflow works on the process preset, on one object, and on filament and printer presets. Later in this guide there is a [candidate catalog](#candidate-catalog): a list of tools we might build, worked out from the product's screens. It follows the implemented catalog record. Nothing in the candidate catalog exists unless the catalog record says it does.
32:- The server starts automatically with the JusPrin Agent panel. There is no `JUSPRIN_MCP` switch to enable it and no bearer token. The server listens only on the numeric loopback address. It prefers port 47301, and falls back to a port chosen by the operating system only when 47301 is taken.
68:- general printing advice that the model can work out from a skill;
75:A fixed, mechanical step of a workflow can be a tool. Examples are generating OrcaSlicer's calibration geometry and starting OrcaSlicer's slice action. Advice should stay a skill until there is a separately specified operation behind it that always behaves the same way.
77:## Skills versus tools
79:A skill is text the model reads. A tool is something the app executes. To decide which one a candidate is, ask one question: does it have to run, or does it only have to be read?
82:- It only has to be read if it is judgement, the order to do things in, facts about printing, how to interpret a tool's result, or which question to ask first. That makes it a skill.
84:The section above covers tools. This section covers skills, and decides the cases that fall in between.
86:A skill contains things the model could do by itself if it had the right knowledge. It contains nothing that executes. Examples:
89:- the order of a series of tool calls, and the reasons for that order. For "make it stronger": read the settings, change walls and infill, slice, read the report;
93:A skill is a file on the Agent page, `AgentUI/src/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`: frontmatter with its `name` and a `trigger`, a `description` or both, then the text the model gets. The page sends every skill once per connection with the `skills` bridge message. A skill with a trigger is the app's: when the event it names happens, the host adds it to the one request where the model first reads about the event, as the request's last item, and to no later request. A skill with a description is the model's: `skill_read` lists the described skills in its own description and returns one by name, and is offered only while at least one exists. One skill has a description and a trigger: `calibration`, read when a print problem may come from the filament or its settings, when the person asks to calibrate, or in a calibration project, and fired by `calibration_started` on the first turn of a calibration project's chat; it carries the conversation of a calibration (when a test is worth it, the two facts said before the person's project closes, asking which test only when the handover leaves it open, per-test ranges and how to read the print, the naming rule for the saved preset), while `calibration_generate`'s description keeps only that tool's rules. Four other skills have triggers, one file each:
95:- `file-loaded` (trigger `file_loaded`): the first message after a file is opened or imported is a judgement about the load report. It fires when the person opens or drops a file, after an in-app `object_import` (and a failed `project_open`) in the same turn, and in the opened project's chat after an in-app `project_open`, which replaces the conversation and so ends the turn that asked. An MCP client's loads fire nothing. The host sends a picture of the active plate with it and, when no purpose is recorded, one sentence of its own built from that state.
96:- `project-setup-changed` (trigger `setup_changed`): check the setup in force against the print's purpose. It fires on the result of an in-app `setup_record` that recorded a purpose for the first time or changed it (its result says which in `purposeChange`; a call that restates the same purpose, or leaves it out, to change the plan does not fire it), when the printer, filament, process or plate type differs from the setup the model was last asked to check under a recorded purpose (on the next tool result of the turn, or on the next turn's first request when the person changed it by hand), on a turn's first request after the person restored an earlier version while a purpose is recorded, and on every turn's first request while the plan is marked `needs_reassessment` (2026-10-28: the model may leave recording the plan to the turn that answers its question about the change, and that turn finds the setup checked already, so without this the mark could outlive every skill that explains it). Each time the model is asked to check, the app saves the setup in force as the one checked. The model's own successful `printer_setup` fires nothing: the setup it chose is saved as checked at once (Kenneth, 2026-10-19), so the skill is for a setup that moved without the model, and a pairing its change breaks is caught by the slice-refusal facts and skill. It gives way to the file-loaded skill on a request that carries both, since that skill already asks for the same check.
97:- `slice-failed` (trigger `slice_failed`): a plate's last slice did not succeed, because OrcaSlicer's check refused the plate or the run failed. The adapter records why on the plate (`WorkspacePlate::slice_failure`: refused or failed, OrcaSlicer's words, the setting and object when named) at the moment it happens (a hook in `Plater::reslice`, `Workspace/SliceRequests.hpp`, and the run's completion event), worded by the print-issue monitor's `slice_failure_of`, and keeps it until the plate slices. The skill fires once per failure, on the first request that carries it: the result of the model's own `slice_start`, the turn the app starts when a slice the model started fails after its turn, or the next message after the person's Slice all. The same refusal again is the same failure.
98:- `print-issues` (trigger `print_issues`): what the print-issue chip's Ask AI button asks for and how to read what OrcaSlicer reports. The adapter reads a slice's warnings through the monitor's `slice_warnings_of` while the plate is active and keeps a summary on the plate while that slice is current (`WorkspacePlate::slice_warnings`: the count, how many the person ignored, and the first warning, critical first, in OrcaSlicer's words with its setting and object). 28:- **Giving the address.** What do they open in a browser, which port, what if the name does not resolve. For a host, this moment happens before the skill arrives, so what the person needs here belongs in the standing prompt or the skill's trigger has to move.
32:For each moment, write what a competent friend would say to someone standing at that screen. That sentence is the skill's job; the error table supports it.
43:The Bambu note was enriched after the 2026-11-02 incident (the plug-in's code, how long it took, a TCP look at port 8883 before and after). That fix was made once and never made a rule; this audit is the rule. Proposed.
47:List every sentence in `printerInstructions.ts` and in the connection tools' descriptions (`Agent/ToolRegistry.cpp`) that gives an exact wording, an exact step or a procedure for connecting. Each one either goes, becomes conditional, or is accepted knowing the skill cannot override it. On 2026-11-04 three such sentences caused failures the skill's facts should have prevented: the "offer it once … with exactly" sentence after `printer_add` (asked a person who had already asked to connect), "say briefly to use that form" after `credential_requested` (told a person with no key to type one), and the finishing example above. The connect tool's "until they give one, ask for it instead of calling this" made the model ask permission to try a port the person had just said to try.
55:Number the steps the connection goes through, each depending on the one before, and say so: a step that worked says nothing about the ones after it. This is what let Sonnet 5.5 reason about failures the skill did not list on 2026-11-03 (an OctoPrint the person called Klipper; `https://` against a plain-http host). Keep the chain from the person's side as well as the app's: for Moonraker, the app reaches Moonraker at its port, and so does the person's browser, so Moonraker's own pages, the key page included, are at that same address and port. The 2026-11-04 skill explained only the app's side, and the model sent the person to a port-80 URL for the key.
59:- **Observed on a real host or printer.** What the app's own test reported, and when (the guard tests in `tests/agent/test_printer_conversation.cpp` require every state the skill names to have a dated run behind it). Write these as facts.
74:Every chat has the provider's web search. Two things are known about it. Offered with no instruction, the model did not search once in four chats (2026-11-02). Told to search before guessing, it searched in two of seven chats and cited its source (2026-11-03). Told to search for the key, it found Moonraker's docs, which give the key page without a port, and handed the person a wrong URL (2026-11-04).

86:- A failed connection: the host's own words, forwarded unchanged ([How to fix a result that hides the failure](mcp-tool-extension-guide.md#how-to-fix-a-result-that-hides-the-failure)), plus what the app itself did and saw: whether a credential was sent, how long the test waited, what a port answered.
88:- The report card: today it is shown at exactly the second failure in a chat (`PrinterConversation::connection_failed`). A 401 after a wrong-port failure counted as the second failure on 2026-11-04 although it was progress. Whether the rule should count repeats of the same outcome instead is open.
102:The 2026-11-03 host chats ran Sonnet 5.5 against Docker hosts with a scripted person who had the key, took the port advice, and knew it was OctoPrint. All seven connected and nothing was learned about guidance. The 2026-11-04 chats ran GPT-5.4 Mini with a person who did not know what an API key was, and failed at every stuck moment.
106:- scripts a person who does **not** have the answer at each stuck moment: no key and no idea what one is; the Mainsail port; a `.local` name; Klipper shut down; the wrong host type;
125:- 2026-10-31, P1S: the app hid a cloud-mode printer and the model invented menus. Tools report what the app saw.

1	# Writing a connection skill
     2	
     3	Draft of 2026-11-04 for Kenneth's review. Nothing here is agreed yet. Where a sentence describes code or a test, it describes what is on `jusprin-newui` at e27c962864; where it proposes a rule, it says so.
     4	
     5	A connection skill is the text the app adds to a printer chat when a person tries to connect a printer of one connection type: `AgentUI/src/skills/connect-bambu/SKILL.md`, `connect-moonraker` and `connect-octoprint`. Read this before writing a new one or changing one. The general rules for skills, and for when a skill becomes a tool, are in [Tool extension guide, Skills versus tools](mcp-tool-extension-guide.md#skills-versus-tools); this document adds only what connecting a printer needs.
     6	
     7	## What the skill is for
     8	
     9	Kenneth's test, 2026-11-02: the skill is good if the agent guides a person who is stuck and makes educated guesses it labels as guesses, until the printer is connected or the person chooses to leave it. It is not judged by whether a printer connected, by how many states it names, or by whether every sentence in it is true. A skill that is never wrong and never helps a stuck person fails the test.
    10	
    11	Three times in three days a skill was written to the wrong half of that test. The first Bambu skill was a table from state to next step, and on the real P1S it told a person with the right access code to re-check it. The second Bambu skill said "add no cause of your own", and the model repeated a false reason instead of guessing. The host skills said "you have not seen where Mainsail or Fluidd show the key", and on 2026-11-04 the model told a person who had no key to look in "Mainsail's settings page", which does not show it. Each time the writer kept "say nothing false" and dropped "help the stuck person".
    12	
    13	## How the skill reaches the model
    14	
    15	Facts about the code today.
    16	
    17	- The app chooses the skill from the connection type and adds it to the conversation once, with the result of the first `printer_connection_status` or `printer_connect` call, or on the first request of a chat opened to connect (`PrinterConversation::connection_skill`, `AgentHost::session_skill`). The model never picks it. For a print host the type is known only from the first `printer_connect`'s `hostType` or a saved connection, so a host skill never arrives before the model has asked for an address and called connect.
    18	- The skill stays in the chat once sent (`AgentSkillUse::stays`).
    19	- Everything before that call runs on the standing prompt alone (`AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts`): the offer to connect after adding, the request for an address, the first connect call. A skill cannot guide those turns.
    20	- The skill opens with "The rules above still apply", so wherever the standing prompt gives an exact sentence or an exact step, the prompt wins over a fact in the skill. On 2026-11-04 the prompt's finishing example "It is connected, so you can send prints straight to it" beat the skill's "verified means Moonraker answered, and nothing more", with Klipper shut down.
    21	
    22	## Before writing: three audits
    23	
    24	### 1. The person's stuck moments, not the app's states
    25	
    26	Start from the moments a person with this connection type gets stuck, and write to those. The failure table (which error text means which step) comes second. The three moments every connection type has:
    27	
    28	- **Giving the address.** What do they open in a browser, which port, what if the name does not resolve. For a host, this moment happens before the skill arrives, so what the person needs here belongs in the standing prompt or the skill's trigger has to move.
    29	- **Being asked for a credential they do not have.** A Klipper owner who has never heard of an API key; a Bambu owner who cannot find the access code. The skill says, in order of cost to check, what is likeliest and what they can look at, each labelled as observed, documented or a guess. The 401-without-a-key case was the one place both 2026-11-04 runs got stuck, and the skill had only "search for where their version shows it".
    30	- **Being told it is connected.** What "verified" proved and did not prove, so the closing sentence does not promise what the app has not checked.
    31	
    32	For each moment, write what a competent friend would say to someone standing at that screen. That sentence is the skill's job; the error table supports it.
    33	
    34	### 2. Information against knowledge, per state
    35	
    36	Kenneth, 2026-11-02: for each failure, is the cause a lack or wrong *information* (a fact about this situation that only the app can know at that moment) or a lack or wrong *knowledge* (how things work)? Information belongs in the app's note or tool result; knowledge about connecting belongs in the skill; how to work in general belongs in the prompt.
    37	
    38	Before writing a line of the skill, list the app's notes for this connection type and, for each, what the app knows at that moment that the model would need. Where the note lacks it, the fix is to the note, and the skill is written against the note that will exist. Examples found on 2026-11-04 for Moonraker:
    39	
    40	- The failure note after HTTP 401 does not say whether the form was submitted empty or with a key, although `PrinterConversation::connect` holds the credential string. The model told a person who typed nothing that "it rejected the key".
    41	- The verified note carries no Klipper state, although `Moonraker::test` reads `klippy_state` from `/server/info` and only logs it. The model said "you can send prints straight to it" to a printer whose Klipper was shut down.
    42	
    43	The Bambu note was enriched after the 2026-11-02 incident (the plug-in's code, how long it took, a TCP look at port 8883 before and after). That fix was made once and never made a rule; this audit is the rule. Proposed.
    44	
    45	### 3. The standing prompt and the tool descriptions
    46	
    47	List every sentence in `printerInstructions.ts` and in the connection tools' descriptions (`Agent/ToolRegistry.cpp`) that gives an exact wording, an exact step or a procedure for connecting. Each one either goes, becomes conditional, or is accepted knowing the skill cannot override it. On 2026-11-04 three such sentences caused failures the skill's facts should have prevented: the "offer it once … with exactly" sentence after `printer_add` (asked a person who had already asked to connect), "say briefly to use that form" after `credential_requested` (told a person with no key to type one), and the finishing example above. The connect tool's "until they give one, ask for it instead of calling this" made the model ask permission to try a port the person had just said to try.
    48	
    49	This matches [Tool extension guide, A tool description versus a skill](mcp-tool-extension-guide.md#skills-versus-tools): a description that has grown into a step belongs in the skill. The skill work added new text and never swept the old. Proposed as a required step.
    50	
    51	## Writing the skill
    52	
    53	### Explain the mechanism as a chain
    54	
    55	Number the steps the connection goes through, each depending on the one before, and say so: a step that worked says nothing about the ones after it. This is what let Sonnet 5.5 reason about failures the skill did not list on 2026-11-03 (an OctoPrint the person called Klipper; `https://` against a plain-http host). Keep the chain from the person's side as well as the app's: for Moonraker, the app reaches Moonraker at its port, and so does the person's browser, so Moonraker's own pages, the key page included, are at that same address and port. The 2026-11-04 skill explained only the app's side, and the model sent the person to a port-80 URL for the key.
    56	
    57	### Three kinds of statement, each labelled
    58	
    59	- **Observed on a real host or printer.** What the app's own test reported, and when (the guard tests in `tests/agent/test_printer_conversation.cpp` require every state the skill names to have a dated run behind it). Write these as facts.
    60	- **Documented.** What a maintainer's docs or FAQ say, named ("Moonraker's docs say…", "Mainsail's FAQ for this error says…"). Write these with their source. The evidence rule does not forbid them; leaving them out is what made the host skills silent about the one thing a stuck Klipper owner needs (that a 401 from a printer on the same home network is usually fixed in `trusted_clients`, with no key at all).
    61	- **A guess.** General knowledge nobody has checked on this setup. Write it as a guess and give the cheapest check.
    62	
    63	What not to write, each from an incident:
    64	
    65	- One next step per state. The state-to-step table sent a person with the right code to re-check it (P1S, 2026-11-02).
    66	- "Add no cause of your own" or anything that forbids reasoning. The model repeated a false reason (P1S, 2026-11-02). The guard bans the phrase.
    67	- A menu path as fact (`Settings > WLAN`). The guard bans arrows and "Settings >".
    68	- A menu path as a presupposition. "Search for where Mainsail shows the key" presupposes it does; the model filled it in with "Mainsail's settings page" (2026-11-04). Say what is known instead: Mainsail and Fluidd do not show it; the two ways to get it; when it is not needed.
    69	- A sentence the standing prompt contradicts with an exact wording. The prompt wins; see audit 3.
    70	- A fix as the single answer. "Restart the printer" became every chat's advice once it was the only untested suggestion listed (P1S, 2026-11-02).
    71	
    72	### Search: say what to look up and how to read it
    73	
    74	Every chat has the provider's web search. Two things are known about it. Offered with no instruction, the model did not search once in four chats (2026-11-02). Told to search before guessing, it searched in two of seven chats and cited its source (2026-11-03). Told to search for the key, it found Moonraker's docs, which give the key page without a port, and handed the person a wrong URL (2026-11-04).
    75	
    76	So the skill names the search for each stuck moment and says how to apply the result to this setup: what the docs assume (Moonraker's default port), what varies by version, and what the model should ask the person to confirm. "Search before you say" alone was not enough.
    77	
    78	### The length
    79	
    80	The skill is read on every request after it arrives. The three skills today are 50 to 60 lines. A stuck-moment section for the credential adds a paragraph, not a page.
    81	
    82	## The app's part
    83	
    84	The skill is only as good as the notes it reads. For each connection type, the notes carry what audit 2 found (proposed; the Bambu note does this today, the host notes do not):
    85	
    86	- A failed connection: the host's own words, forwarded unchanged ([How to fix a result that hides the failure](mcp-tool-extension-guide.md#how-to-fix-a-result-that-hides-the-failure)), plus what the app itself did and saw: whether a credential was sent, how long the test waited, what a port answered.
    87	- A verified connection: what the app checked and anything it read on the way that bears on the next step, such as Klipper's state.
    88	- The report card: today it is shown at exactly the second failure in a chat (`PrinterConversation::connection_failed`). A 401 after a wrong-port failure counted as the second failure on 2026-11-04 although it was progress. Whether the rule should count repeats of the same outcome instead is open.
    89	
    90	## Testing a connection skill
    91	
    92	### Offline, today
    93	
    94	- `tests/agent/test_printer_conversation.cpp`: the skill arrives only once the type is known and never in a chat that only adds a printer; every state named in backquotes has a dated real run; banned phrases are absent.
    95	- `AgentUI/src/skills.test.ts` and `wording.test.ts`: the file parses, the trigger is unique, the text says "the app" and never "arrives".
    96	- The shell harness's `--print-host-check` (hosts) and `--printer-connect-skill` (the P1S): the app's own connection test against a real host or printer with no model, the source of every "observed" line.
    97	
    98	These prove where the skill arrives and that its facts were seen. They say nothing about whether its words help.
    99	
   100	### Live, with Kenneth's test
   101	
   102	The 2026-11-03 host chats ran Sonnet 5.5 against Docker hosts with a scripted person who had the key, took the port advice, and knew it was OctoPrint. All seven connected and nothing was learned about guidance. The 2026-11-04 chats ran GPT-5.4 Mini with a person who did not know what an API key was, and failed at every stuck moment.
   103	
   104	So a live run of a connection skill (proposed):
   105	
   106	- scripts a person who does **not** have the answer at each stuck moment: no key and no idea what one is; the Mainsail port; a `.local` name; Klipper shut down; the wrong host type;
   107	- runs on the weakest model the product offers by default, not only on the model the writer prefers;
   108	- is judged by where the person ends up (`ended_badly` in `tests/printer_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py`), including the closing sentence, not by whether the printer connected;
   109	- reads the transcript as the model saw it, every tool call, result and note in order, before any line of the skill is changed, and names for each failure the text the model saw or lacked.
   110	
   111	Live runs cost money and need Kenneth's approval of a specific batch with a token estimate.
   112	
   113	## Checklist before a connection skill is committed
   114	
   115	1. The three stuck moments are written to, each with labelled guesses in order of cost.
   116	2. Audit 2 is written down: for each note, what the app knows and what the note says; the gaps are fixed or listed.
   117	3. Audit 3 is written down: every exact connecting sentence in the prompt and the tool descriptions, and what was done with it.
   118	4. Every state in backquotes has a dated real run; the guard passes.
   119	5. Every documented claim names its source; every guess says it is one; no menu is stated or presupposed.
   120	6. Each search the skill asks for says what to search and how to apply the answer.
   121	7. A stuck-person live run on the default model, approved and run, with the transcript read before any edit.
   122	
   123	## Where the rules come from
   124	
   125	- 2026-10-31, P1S: the app hid a cloud-mode printer and the model invented menus. Tools report what the app saw.
   126	- 2026-11-01: "a general process that improves when more people are using it" (Kenneth); tool results carry what is true now, a skill carries how it works.
   127	- 2026-11-02: the state-to-step table failed on the real P1S; "guide the user… make educated guess"; "the goal here is not to connect my printer"; information against knowledge, and where each belongs.
   128	- 2026-11-02 to 03: web search alone was never used; told to search, the model did, in some chats.
   129	- 2026-11-03: the host skills were written from Docker evidence and proven with a person who knew the answers; "apply the lessons" was done from memory, and search was left out of them by mistake.
   130	- 2026-11-04: two live Moonraker runs on GPT-5.4 Mini failed at each stuck moment. Diagnosis and lessons review in the side-session notes of 2026-11-04 (`moonraker-skill-diagnosis.md`, `connection-skill-lessons-review.md`).

The adapter records why on the plate (`WorkspacePlate::slice_failure`: refused or failed, OrcaSlicer's words, the setting and object when named) at the moment it happens (a hook in `Plater::reslice`, `Workspace/SliceRequests.hpp`, and the run's completion event), worded by the print-issue monitor's `slice_failure_of`, and keeps it until the plate slices. Every request carries it as the plate's `sliceFailure`; `slice_report` of an unsliced plate adds the check code and the object's name. The same refusal again is the same failure.

The adapter reads a slice's warnings through the monitor's `slice_warnings_of` while the plate is active and keeps a summary on the plate while that slice is current (`WorkspacePlate::slice_warnings`: the count, how many the person ignored, and the first warning, critical first, in OrcaSlicer's words with its setting and object). It counts every warning the chip lists. The chip and `slice_report` read the same slice-result rule (`Workspace/SliceResultWarnings`), so they list the same warnings, except that `slice_report` also lists the timelapse ones, marked `appliesWhen: "timelapse"`, which the chip does not count. Every request carries it as the plate's `sliceWarnings`. The skill fires on the request that carries a chip's message, and on the first request whose workspace shows warnings no request has carried yet, whether the person sliced (their next message) or the model did (the tool result that shows them, or the app's turn when its slice ended after its turn); a re-slice with the same warnings fires nothing.
 
+The connection skills (`connect-bambu`, `connect-moonraker`, `connect-octoprint`) have rules of their own, in [Writing a connection skill](connection-skill-guide.md) (draft, under review).
+
 The cases in between:
 
 - **A procedure made of existing tool calls.** It is a skill for as long as carrying it out takes judgement. It becomes a tool only when the steps are fixed and the person wants the whole thing as one action that can be undone. If there are many such fixed sequences, they go in one workflow registry (see [When resources or skills are appropriate](#when-resources-or-skills-are-appropriate)).

    14	
    15	Facts about the code today.
    16

    19	- Everything before that call runs on the standing prompt alone (`AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts`): the offer to connect after adding, the request for an address, the first connect call. A skill cannot guide those turns.

    23	
    24	### 1. The person's stuck moments, not the app's states
    25	
    26	Start from the moments a person with this connection type gets stuck, and write to those. The failure table (which error text means which step) comes second. The three moments every connection type has:
    27	
    28	- **Giving the address.** What do they open in a browser, which port, what if the name does not resolve. For a host, this moment happens before the skill arrives, so what the person needs here belongs in the standing prompt or the skill's trigger has to move.
    29	- **Being asked for a credential they do not have.** A Klipper owner who has never heard of an API key; a Bambu owner who cannot find the access code.
